title: The first 24 hours after fraud
body_md:
## Sort the damage before you watch the clock

The transfer left your account an hour ago, the person at the other end of the chat has gone quiet, and you are rereading the messages for the tenth time. Do two things first: stop replying to that person, and stop paying. Then work out what was actually taken.

“First 24 hours” is a nudge to move. It is not a legal deadline, and beating it guarantees nothing. What matters is the kind of damage, because each kind has its own fix: someone used your card, you were talked into approving a transfer, you sent cryptocurrency, you gave away a password, or a stranger got into your phone or computer. If anyone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number first.

### Money: ask by payment type

Phone your bank, card issuer, transfer app or exchange through a channel you found yourself, never one the scammer supplied. Ask what can be blocked, disputed, recalled or reversed for your kind of payment. A card billing error and a transfer you authorized are handled differently, and a recall can fail. With crypto, note the transaction hash, receiving address, asset, amount and time. The blockchain transfer itself is generally irreversible, though your exchange or wallet provider may have options. Get a case number and note the next deadline.

### Passwords and devices

If you gave away a password, use the service’s genuine recovery flow. Change that password and every other one that matches it, check the open sessions, and turn on stronger sign-in where it is offered. If someone had remote access, end the session and get help from someone you trust who knows devices; if the device itself may be compromised, recover your accounts from a clean one. If identity data got out, follow your own country’s official identity-theft process, not a credit-freeze checklist written for another.

### Evidence and reports

Keep the original messages, receipts, dates and screenshots somewhere private. The US IC3’s FAQ asks for transaction details and, where relevant, the original email headers; it takes no attachments, so the originals stay with you. Report to the proper authority where you live, but do not wait for a police number before telling the payment provider. Be wary of anyone who offers to recover your money for a fee. If you have been told to keep quiet, or you are too embarrassed to talk, tell someone you trust anyway: you were deceived by people who do this for a living, and that is no reason to put off asking for help.

widget_config.goal: After suspected fraud, choose your next safe move by what was exposed and how the money left.
widget_config.today_action: Copy your bank’s fraud contact, the steps to freeze your card and the recovery pages for your main accounts from the official apps or sites, and keep them somewhere private.
widget_config.scope: A teaching sequence, not a legal clock: no universal rule gives you 24 hours. The FTC and IC3 procedures apply in the US, the Bank of Russia card steps in Russia. The people and sites in the cases are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FTC: What To Do if You Were Scammed
sources.scope: What to tell your payment provider and how to secure your accounts, for US readers. Recovery is not guaranteed.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Complaint FAQ
sources.scope: How US complaints are filed and what evidence to keep. IC3 does not accept attachments.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Cryptocurrency
sources.scope: US reporting, and the transaction details worth recording. Blockchain transfers generally cannot be reversed.

sources.title: Bank of Russia: Unauthorized Card Debits
sources.scope: The steps for a Russian cardholder facing an unauthorized debit. It is not a promise of automatic refund.

blocks.title: A second payment to “release” the balance
blocks.situation: Noor wired money yesterday to what she was told was an investment account. Tonight the site asks for a second payment to release her balance and says the account will close at midnight.
blocks.analysis: Stop paying, and call the bank that sent the transfer today to ask about a recall. Keep the transfer record and the chat. Do not wait until you know who really owns the site. A recall may still come to nothing, but every day of delay narrows the options.

blocks.title: Two hotel lines for one stay
blocks.situation: Two hotel entries sit in your card app: a deposit and the final room charge, one of them marked pending. You phone the front desk on the number from the hotel’s own site, and the clerk explains the temporary authorization and sends you a receipt.
blocks.analysis: A pending authorization can drop away without ever becoming a second settled charge. Keep the receipt, watch the final statement, and call your issuer only if both amounts settle or the figure is wrong. Asking questions is reasonable. Calling it fraud over a hold is not.

blocks.title: The delivery page that took too much
blocks.setup: An invented scenario. A fake parcel-delivery page talked you into typing a password you also use elsewhere and approving a small card payment. An hour later a charge you do not recognize appears on the card.

steps.prompt: The page is still open, and its chat window is offering to “verify” your card. What do you do with that conversation?

choices.text: Close the page and the chat, and refuse any “verification” payment.
choices.consequence: The scammer loses the easiest route to a second payment.
choices.explanation: Paying a new fee cannot vouch for the old transaction.

choices.text: Ask the page’s operator to refund the charge, after paying the extra fee they ask for.
choices.consequence: You may end up paying the same people twice.
choices.explanation: Only your real issuer can deal with the charge, never the suspicious page.

steps.prompt: Now there are two charges on the card: the small one you approved and one you do not recognize. Whom do you tell?

choices.text: Whoever answers the support number on the fake delivery page.
choices.consequence: The scammer may collect more of your card details.
choices.explanation: Reach the issuer by a route you find yourself.

choices.text: The issuer, through its app or the number on your card, describing the two charges separately.
choices.consequence: The issuer can freeze the card and tell you which dispute route fits each charge.
choices.explanation: Each charge needs its own accurate label, because the route depends on it.

steps.prompt: The password you typed is one you use on other sites too. What do you do about it?

choices.text: Delete the fake page from your browser history.
choices.consequence: The password still works for whoever collected it.
choices.explanation: Clearing history does not change a password.

choices.text: On the real services, change it everywhere you reused it, then check open sessions and two-step sign-in.
choices.consequence: The old password stops working on every service where you had reused it.
choices.explanation: One exposed password endangers every place it was reused.

steps.prompt: What do you keep, and where does it go?

choices.text: Keep the original message, receipts, dates and the bank’s case number privately, and report through your country’s official route.
choices.consequence: You can lay out what happened, in order, without putting details in public.
choices.explanation: Tell the payment provider first. Do not wait for a report to be filed.

choices.text: Post screenshots of your account and card to ask for help.
choices.consequence: Sensitive details can spread, and recovery scammers read public posts.
choices.explanation: Evidence belongs in private, protected channels.

blocks.debrief: Each hole gets its own repair: the payments stop, the provider hears first, the reused password changes, the evidence stays private. “24 hours” is a nudge, not an expiry date. Play it again with the answers you skipped and see what each would have cost.

questions.prompt: You approved a bank transfer because you were deceived. Does that automatically give you a card chargeback?

choices.text: No. Ask the sending bank promptly about a recall and whatever else it can do.
choices.explanation: Transfers and card disputes run on different procedures.

choices.text: Yes. Every payment can be reversed in the same way.
choices.explanation: Your rights depend on the payment method and the country.

questions.prompt: You have the transaction hash of a crypto transfer. What is it good for?

choices.text: Reversing the transaction on the blockchain right away.
choices.explanation: A confirmed blockchain transfer normally cannot be reversed.

choices.text: Documenting the transfer for your provider and for the authorities.
choices.explanation: A hash is evidence. It is not a key that undoes anything.

questions.prompt: After you post about your loss, a stranger offers to recover the money for a fee. What do you do?

choices.text: Send the deposit; they clearly know your case.
choices.explanation: Anyone can read a public post and repeat what is in it.

choices.text: Decline, and go to your real provider and the official reporting channels.
choices.explanation: An unsolicited request for a fee is how people lose money a second time.
